subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Women's Petition Against Coffee
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Women's Petition Against Coffee.

hook.text: In 1674, London women published 'The Women's Petition Against Coffee,' complaining their husbands spent all day in coffeehouses.

buildup.text: The petition claimed coffee made men impotent, lazy, and absent from home. Wives were fed up with empty beds and cold dinners.

discovery.text: Men responded with 'The Men's Answer'—arguing that coffee improved their stamina and intellect, making them better husbands.

twist.text: The petitions were likely satirical—18th-century social commentary disguised as a gender battle. But the social tension was real.

climax.text: Charles II tried banning coffeehouses in 1675. The ban lasted just 11 days before public outcry reversed it.

punchline.text: Women protested, the king banned, the people revolted. Coffee was unstoppable.

quiz.question: How long did King Charles II's 1675 coffeehouse ban last?
options: Just 11 days before public outcry reversed it

details.summary: In 1674, London women published a petition complaining that their husbands spent too much time and money in coffeehouses, neglecting home and family. The satirical document argued that coffee was making men impotent and useless. Men responded with their own counter-petition.
details.whyItMatters: The Women's Petition reveals the social disruption coffeehouses caused in 17th-century London, where they functioned as men-only spaces that excluded women from public intellectual life.
takeaways: London women petitioned against coffeehouses in 1674
They argued coffee caused male neglect of family duties
The episode highlights the gendered nature of early coffeehouse culture

faq.question: Was the Women's Petition Against Coffee a serious political document?
faq.answer: Most historians consider it partly satirical, though it reflected genuine frustrations. The petition used humor and exaggeration, but the underlying complaints about men's absence from home were very real in 1670s London.

faq.question: Were women actually banned from English coffeehouses in the 1600s?
faq.answer: Women were not formally banned but were effectively excluded by strong social custom. Coffeehouses were male-dominated spaces for business and politics. Women who ran coffeehouses as proprietors were a notable exception.
